corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26.2; go test -run '^$' -bench . -benchmem -count=10 (default Go build flags), ten samples per version interleaved and compared for significance; eligible integer loop traces compile to native code on Windows/amd64 and Linux/amd64, other platforms use a portable typed Go executor
corrections.caveats: The 249.71x headline is BenchmarkMainLoop (runtime_test.go), an empty 'for (var i=0; i<100000; i++) {}' loop over a global variable, and global_counter_trace.go is a dedicated lowering for exactly that empty global integer counter loop shape: it keeps the counter in a Go integer (with a per-iteration interrupt check) and writes the property back on exit. The result is semantically correct and the loop still runs (about 1 ns per iteration), but the headline is a special case built for the benchmark's own shape and says little about general code. The other significant rows are 1.39x-2.86x (call boundary and VM dispatch micro benchmarks) and 48 of 55 shared benchmarks did not change significantly. Raw benchstat output is not published, only the summary table. The benchjs suite compares the same JS workloads with V8 but publishes no results; V8 would be far faster on compute. Independent fork with two stars and a separate module path (github.com/maclof/goja-perf), so its Goja values are distinct Go types from upstream's and goja_nodejs needs an adapter. Measured on one Windows laptop CPU.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly and the MainLoop benchmark source is identical upstream, so the comparison is fair as measured; the shortcoming is that the 249.71x row comes from global_counter_trace.go, an optimization that matches only the empty global counter loop the benchmark uses. tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md carries every quoted number for Apple M4 and Intel Xeon D-2123IT against C SQLite (mattn/go-sqlite3 v1.14.48, pinned in compat-harness/go.mod) and Turso, from the public harness compat-harness/bench_columnar_vs_c_test.go (TestBenchColumnarVsC) with the exact go test command and BENCH_SKIP list; the harness checks every arm's answers against C SQLite before timing. Go 1.27.0 comes from go.mod (the page itself names no toolchain or cgo C compiler versions), which matches the wazy precedent for this author's Go harnesses.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.27.0 per go.mod and compat-harness/go.mod (the benchmark page states no toolchain version); default go test build; C SQLite is mattn/go-sqlite3 v1.14.48 built through cgo with default flags (C compiler not stated); Turso via turso.tech/database/tursogo v0.7.2; harness compat-harness/bench_columnar_vs_c_test.go (TestBenchColumnarVsC), JIT on vs MUSQL_JIT=0
corrections.caveats: The published run sets BENCH_SKIP to drop 17 read shapes that no musql fast path answers (min/max, GROUP BY with HAVING, OR, BETWEEN, IN list, IS NULL, LIKE, ORDER BY text, group_concat, DISTINCT, subqueries, EXISTS, UNION, OFFSET, join projecting) plus every write (UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE); the harness's own comments say those shapes run the ordinary VDBE, which trails C SQLite by about 3.5x on a scan, and that writes are where the engine is at its worst, so the published table shows the JIT-served shapes plus three point lookups only. The win comes from columnar storage plus JIT against SQLite's row store (musql reads its own .musq format after VACUUM; SQLite files need conversion); without the JIT musql is much slower than C SQLite on the same scans (9.83 ms vs 2.17 ms for the one-predicate filtered count on M4). Arms are not identical: musql is timed through its direct engine API while C SQLite is timed through database/sql and cgo with each result rendered to a string, which matters only for the microsecond rows. Whole-table count is answered from segments' recorded row counts, not a scan. Microsecond-scale rows vary run to run, more on amd64. The README headline 75x is the two-machine average of the one-predicate (73x) and two-predicate (77x) rows. The repository history is a single squashed commit (2026-10-05).

notes: Numbers and ratios match docs/benchmarks.md row for row, and results are checked against C SQLite before timing, so the evidence is valid; the main shortcoming is a cherry-picked published table (BENCH_SKIP removes the non-JIT read shapes where musql trails C SQLite by about 3.5x, and all writes). Apache-2.0, 29 stars, 3 forks, one commit on main dated 2026-10-05; arguably a database engine more than a JIT, category left as filed.

tier_reason: The cross-language table in docs/performance.md is reproducible on paper (perf-results/docker/Dockerfile, perf-results/docker/run_all_benchmarks.sh, perf-results/cross-lang/benchmarks/*, obr built with -O3 -flto=auto -mavx2 per core/vm/make/Makefile.amd64, Ryzen 9 7950X3D), but the headline win over LuaJIT compares different algorithms: Objeck runs programs/tests/clbg/fannkuchredux.obs, the optimized CLBG algorithm in a native-annotated (always JIT-compiled) function, while LuaJIT runs perf-results/cross-lang/benchmarks/fannkuchredux.lua, a naive full-reversal port that allocates a fresh table for every permutation. A baseline column that ran a weaker program caps the evidence at C (v8malloc precedent).

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/performance.md (2026-09-12 Docker run, median of 3): binarytrees 17 Objeck 2.14 s vs LuaJIT 3.57 s (1.7x faster, the one like-for-like win) and Java 21 0.26 s; nbody 50M Objeck 8.14 s vs LuaJIT 4.37 s and Java 2.35 s (slower); spectralnorm 5500 Objeck 2.72 s vs LuaJIT 1.12 s and Java 1.18 s (slower); fannkuchredux 12 Objeck 32.76 s vs LuaJIT 117.99 s (page says 3.6x faster) and Java 20.70 s, but that row is not like-for-like because Objeck runs the optimized CLBG algorithm and LuaJIT a naive port that allocates a table per permutation. Objeck beats CPython 3.12 and Ruby 3.2 on all four rows (for example nbody 16.6x and 27.0x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Objeck v2026.9.1 (f6b3b09046), VM (obr) and compiler (obc) built from source in Ubuntu 24.04 with g++ from build-essential using core/vm/make/Makefile.amd64 (-O3 -flto=auto -mavx2 -std=c++20); programs compiled with -opt s3; LuaJIT, Python 3.12.3, Ruby 3.2.3 and OpenJDK 21.0.12 from Ubuntu apt packages (perf-results/docker/Dockerfile); Objeck timed with /usr/bin/time %e, the other languages with date +%s%N around each process
corrections.caveats: The Lua source behind the 117.99 s LuaJIT fannkuchredux time (perf-results/cross-lang/benchmarks/fannkuchredux.lua) creates a new table with 'local perm = {}' and copies 12 elements into it for every permutation (hundreds of millions of table allocations and resizes for n=12) and reverses from index 0, whereas the Java port reuses one preallocated array and Objeck's programs/tests/clbg/fannkuchredux.obs is the optimized CLBG algorithm (first-element swap trick, reversal of the inner span only) inside a native-annotated function; the Python and Ruby ports are the same naive algorithm. The 3.6x fannkuchredux win over LuaJIT therefore measures a weaker Lua program, not LuaJIT, and Java, running the naive algorithm, still beats Objeck on it. The Java and Python ports also compute the checksum sign from the checksum's parity rather than the permutation index, and every program's output goes to /dev/null unchecked. Like-for-like rows: Objeck beats LuaJIT only on binarytrees (1.7x) and loses on nbody (1.9x) and spectralnorm (2.4x); Java wins 3 of 4 rows. Only four benchmarks are in the cross-language table, all in Docker on a Windows 11 host; LuaJIT is the distro package with the exact build not recorded. Objeck is a language VM with a JIT, not a drop-in library. The most recent commit seen was a bot download-stats snapshot (2026-10-05); the last code commits are 2026-10-03 and release notes for v2026.10.0 were added on 2026-10-02, while the repo page shows v2026.9.7 as the latest release.

notes: Inspected the Lua source as asked: fannkuchredux.lua allocates a fresh table per permutation and uses a naive algorithm, while Objeck runs the optimized CLBG program, so the 3.6x 'beats LuaJIT' headline is not like-for-like; downgraded A to C rather than rejected because the remaining rows are genuine and Objeck's binarytrees win (1.7x) uses comparable programs. Record shortcomings: not faster than LuaJIT on like-for-like float rows, not faster than Java on 3 of 4, unequal baseline port on the headline row.
